extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of advertising history; advertisers and journalists interested in historical practices and ethical standards
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts norms, practices, and evaluative comments about 19th-century advertisements and newspaper-advertising ethics from a chapter of a history of advertising. Emphasises propriety, editorial/advertising separation, tactics used in adverts, and examples of acceptable/objectionable forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decency / propriety in advertisements
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers should refuse many notices which are indecent or improper; 'a sense of what is right and proper compels them to refuse many notices which would be highly paid for.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: family papers forbidding use of the name of the Deity in advertising; editors rejecting advertisements that would be 'beyond reproach' for high-class papers. The text argues that newspapers ought to prioritize decency over immediate profit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of exploiting private misfortunes
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertising that attempts 'to make profit out of others' misfortunes' is criticised as a sharp or objectionable bit of business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a linen-draper issuing a large handbill with a mourning border and sale of bankrupt man's stock; labelled by the author as morally dubious and 'worthy of the hero of the wooden nutmegs.' This is presented as an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthfulness and honesty in pricing and claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisements and sellers should avoid deceptive practices such as making up 'two sets of figures' on goods; accurate representation of market vs offered prices is implied as a standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author notes that producing two sets of figures 'has been found very efficacious' but treats this as a questionable practice; recommendation is implicit to avoid such deception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and verification of circulation claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertising contracts and claims about circulation should be verifiable: only count papers actually sold and paid for; require sworn affidavits from pressman, delivery clerk, and cashier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted proposition from the New York Daily News: three cents per line per ten thousand circulation with each bill accompanied by sworn affidavits and only counting sold/paid copies. Presented as 'fair and equitable.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation (and integrity) between editorial matter and paid advocacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspapers should avoid mixing paid advocacy with editorial opinion; open announcements that columns 'are to be bought' are condemned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: journals that publish paid advocacy or allegedly sell their opinions are criticised. Editorial 'puffs' or personal advertisements used to run tradesmen's praise are noted as problematic practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial notices should be practical and not thinly-disguised ads
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors should limit editorial responses to 'practical and useful' queries rather than answer trivial matters that serve as thinly-veiled advertorials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a Yankee editor declines to answer a query about a broom used in a novel but would promptly name the best hatter — showing the expectation that editorial space be used practically, not as paid promotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of immoral or corrupt classified content
rubrics_metrics.description: Classified and matrimonial columns should be policed to prevent facilitating vice or 'shameful advertisements' that may ruin people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Mercury's 'Matrimonial' adverts are cited as facilitating prostitution or immorality; the author argues such columns can have real moral consequences and should be judged critically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain an outward show of decency for family papers
rubrics_metrics.description: For papers aiming at family readership, maintain an 'outward and visible show of decency' in the advertisement columns even if content beneath might be questionable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author contrasts British practice of outward decency with American 'broader notions' and suggests family papers should preserve visible propriety so they can be left on breakfast-tables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use humour and novelty judiciously
rubrics_metrics.description: Humour and cleverness in advertising are effective and desirable, but should avoid unpleasantness or tastelessness; 'it is possible to be wise as well as witty.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: witty American adverts (graveyard fence 'Use Jones's bottled ale if you would keep out of here') praised; but much American advertising is also criticised for vulgar or scurrilous humour. Use of blank space as an ironic ad is cited as clever.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate length and breadth for advertisements
rubrics_metrics.description: Ads should be of a suitable length and scope; sometimes 'they are too long for quotation, at other times they are too broad.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author notes difficulty in dealing with American advertisements because of excessive length or broadness; implies that advertisers should tailor copy length to medium and audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid selling editorial favour or blackmail
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspapers or journals that openly state their columns 'are to be bought' or use blackmailing qualities are unethical and diminish journalistic integrity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: San Francisco Newsletter is cited as having informed the world its 'opinions and advocacy are within easy purchase'; the history condemns this practice and describes its effects on ability and tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advert copy should include clear sale logistics and terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Sale advertisements should state precise dates, times, terms, modes of sale (e.g., 'by Private Treaty'), and any special arrangements for attendees (e.g., entrance by private door for ladies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example handbill: lists sale days, 'From Ten a.m. till Dusk each Day, closing on Thursday, at 5 p.m., prompt, not a minute later,' and 'The Sale will be by Private Treaty... No OFFER WILL BE REJECTED, AS EVERYTHING MUST BE SOLD IN THE BRIEF TIME SPECIFIED.' These are presented as practical features of sale adverts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid tasteless exploitation in tone and imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Using morbid, indecent, or tasteless imagery or appeals (e.g., 'Port wine as pure as the tears which fall upon a sister's grave' or coffin/mattress juxtaposition) is noted as distasteful and morally questionable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author catalogs numerous examples of American adverts that choose grave subjects or funeral language for commercial effect and treats many as examples of lax propriety; advises caution in tone selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement and integration tactics (mixing ads with editorial matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some papers spread puffs and notices among ordinary matter (ads in 'backs' and 'gutters' or integrated with copy) as a distinctive construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The San Francisco Newsletter's practice of distributing advertisements through page margins and mixing puffs with editorial content is described as 'unique' but also as contributing to a deterioration of tone; presented as a tactic rather than endorsement.
